titre: The Cantillon Effect, or Why New Money Doesn't Enrich Everyone Equally
accroche: In the 18th century, a banker describes how new money never reaches everyone at the same time, and why that decides who gets rich.
contenu_vulgarise:
Richard Cantillon writes, around 1730, a manuscript that circulates clandestinely for a quarter of a century before being published in 1755 under the title *Essai sur la nature du commerce en général* (*Essay on the Nature of Commerce in General*): twenty-one years after the death of its author, in a London fire in May 1734 that was never fully explained. An Irish banker based in Paris, Cantillon himself profited from the collapse of Law's system in 1720: he had bought shares in the Mississippi Company early, to resell them at the peak, then lent at high rates to debtors ruined by the crash. From this he draws a theory of money more refined than that of his time.

## Money never arrives everywhere at once

The English philosopher John Locke had already noticed that more abundant money drives prices up, without explaining how. Cantillon fills this gap: a quantity of new money, he writes, never appears uniformly spread across an economy, it always enters at a specific point. If it comes from a mine, those who receive it first are, he says in his text, “the owner of these mines, the entrepreneurs, the smelters, the refiners, and generally all those who work in them.” Cantillon describes these newly rich with an image that has remained famous: “They will consume more meat and more wine or beer in their households than they did before.” This new demand pushes up the prices of the products it targets first, well before the money has finished circulating to the last hands that receive it. Those people face prices that have already risen with an income that has not yet moved: they grow relatively poorer, while the first to be served grow richer. Cantillon draws a remark from this that contrasts with the simple quantity theory of his day: doubling the quantity of money in a state doesn't necessarily double the prices of goods and merchandise, because how the money circulates matters as much as how much of it there is.

## An effect that didn't wait to be given a name

The name “Cantillon effect” appears only long after the author; more recent economists adopted it to name what he had observed from the start, in a language that was not yet that of economics as a separate discipline. The shift he proposes remains relevant every time a central bank injects new money into an economy: the channel through which this money enters (bond market, banking sector, public spending) determines who benefits first, and at what prices those who receive it early adjust first. What Cantillon saw from a Parisian bank in the 18th century still holds: monetary policy is never neutral between those who receive the money early and those who receive it, at best, only after prices have already climbed.

carte.punch: The same increase in money doesn't enrich everyone at the same time.
carte.idee: Around 1730, the banker Richard Cantillon describes how new money always arrives at a specific point of an economy (a mine, a bank) and first enriches those who get it first, while the last to be served face prices that have already risen without their income having moved.
carte.source_courte: Cantillon, *Essai sur le commerce* (*Essay on Commerce*), 1755

quiz.question: According to Cantillon, why doesn't an increase in the quantity of money in a state benefit everyone equally?
choix: Because the new money is always hoarded by the state before being put into circulation
Because new money enters at a specific point, and those who receive it first push prices up before everyone else
Because only mine owners have the right to spend newly created money
Because the quantity of money in circulation actually has no effect on the prices of goods
quiz.explication: Cantillon describes a gradual and unequal diffusion: those who get the new money first spend more and push up certain prices, before this money reaches the last to be served, who face the price increase without their income having risen yet.

quiz_supplementaire.question: How did Cantillon personally profit from the collapse of Law's system in 1720?
choix: By buying shares in the Mississippi Company early, then lending to ruined debtors
By being appointed by the Regency to liquidate the assets of Law's bank after its bankruptcy
By selling his stake in Law's system in advance, even before its official launch
By borrowing heavily from Law's bank to speculate on Spanish silver mines
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Cantillon bought shares in the Mississippi Company early to resell them at the peak, then lent at high rates to debtors ruined by the 1720 crash.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Which philosopher had already noticed, before Cantillon, that more abundant money drives prices up, without explaining how?
choix: David Hume, in a treatise on the circulation of English money
Adam Smith, in a chapter devoted to the Mississippi Company
John Locke, whose incomplete observation Cantillon completes
John Law, in the public defense of his own monetary system
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The text attributes this earlier observation to the English philosopher John Locke, which Cantillon completes by explaining the mechanism of the unequal diffusion of new money.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Was the name “Cantillon effect” given by Cantillon himself to his observation?
choix: Yes, he uses it explicitly in his 1755 *Essai sur le commerce*
No, more recent economists named it that long after him
No, it was John Locke who coined this expression in his lifetime
Yes, but only in a private letter found after his death
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The name appears long after the author: more recent economists adopted it to name what Cantillon had observed in a language still lacking a separate economic vocabulary.
